newsitem.title: CROATIA: Croatia '96 C/A gap seen shrinking to 7 pct of GDP.
newsitem.headline: Croatia '96 C/A gap seen shrinking to 7 pct of GDP.

text.p: Croatia's 1996 current account gap, although still relatively large, may shrink to around seven percent of gross domestic product from 10 percent in 1995, central bank analyst Velimir Sonje said on Thursday.
Nominal gross domestic product (GDP) estimates for last year range from 99 to 103 billion kuna ($17.6 billion).
"Based on the trade figures for the last quarter (1996), we can put the current account deficit at some $1.2-1.3 billion," Sonje told Reuters in an interview and added:
"More importantly, I believe it is sustainable."

The current account gap reached $745 million in the January-September, according to preliminary figures, down some 35 percent from the first nine months of 1995, he said. Figures have been delayed due to a new accounting system introduced in mid-1996.
As Croatia's imports soared to support a post-war recovery, its trade gap widened to a record $3.28 billion in 1996, the increase totalling 13.9 percent from a year earlier.
But it was partly compensated by a surplus in services, such as transport and tourism, worth $937 million in the first nine months, Sonje said.
Services brought Croatia $525 million income in the same period of 1995 -- the last year of conflicts with separatist Serbs and of an all-out war in neighbouring Bosnia.
Tourist trade, the country's main currency earner, picked up considerably with a comeback of foreign holidaymakers after a wide peace accord was internationally brokered late in 1995.

Sonje cited larger money transfers from 'aunts' and 'uncles' -- Croats living and working abroad -- and continued mobilisation of people's currency savings as also offsetting part of the trade gap last year.

These savings, that no one can put a figure on with any degree of certainty, have been hoarded under the mattresses for decades due to distrust of the banking system. Many citizens still keep them in foreign bank accounts.
"There is no way of knowing how large they are. If you conducted a survey, I doubt many people would tell you," Sonje said.

Although declining in comparison with war years when other governments poured humanitarian aid into Croatia and also financed various other projects, state sector transfers were still a help in 1996, he added.

As confidence in the economy grew, last year saw much higher foreign investment on the financial account side of the balance of payments. Direct foreign investments rose fivefold to almost $250 million to last August.
The National Bank of Croatia's currency reserves also rose to $2.3 billion at the end of 1996, compared to zero when the country gained independence in 1991.
Officials argue the government has not borrowed so much abroad to make its struggling post-war economy overindebted.
However, both the central bank and some independent analyst are cautioning against an unbridled fiscal expansion that would push Croatia deeper into debt or render servicing unbearable.
Foreign debt, including Croatia's share of old Yugoslav liabilities rescheduled at comfortable terms, is put at 26 percent of GDP at the moment.
